1.pericope_label: And Bezaleel made the ark of shittim wood: two cubits and a half was the length of it, and a cubit and a half the breadth of it, and a cubit and a half the height of it: And he overlaid it with pure gold within and without, and made a crown of gold to it round about.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin divide the ground between them. Gill takes up why the work is credited to Bezaleel alone: Jarchi explained it by his having given his mind to the work more than the rest of the wise men, and some Jewish writers inferred that he made the ark unaided — which Gill rejects, because the mercy seat, the cherubim, the shewbread table, the candlestick, the two altars and the laver of brass are ascribed to him in exactly the same way, and are called his because they were made by his direction and under his oversight; from Aben Ezra he adds that the singular ascription stands here particularly for the glory of the ark. Calvin answers the repetition by pointing to the wording: the execution is narrated in almost the identical terms as the command, so that we may see the artificers did not vary in the smallest point — not a syllable of the table neglected, the candlestick, the incense altar and the oil all answering exactly. The lesson he draws is that Moses commends obedience as the foundation of true piety, and shows that no imagination was exercised anywhere in the tabernacle service, nothing being more opposed to the purity of religion than doing what is not enjoined.

Henry treats the repetition as the chapter’s real difficulty and answers it directly. It might have sufficed for Moses to say in a few words that everything was made according to the directions already recorded; but scripture has no idle words and no vain repetitions, so the length must be purposeful. He gives two reasons. Moses wrote first for Israel, who were never allowed to see the furniture of the tabernacle — that was the priests’ privilege alone — and what they could not look upon had therefore to be set before them in words. And what we most need to take in is written more than once, exactly as several of the evangelists relate the same passages of the history of Christ; the great things of the law and the gospel need to be inculcated upon us again and again.

Ellicott contributes a single restriction, and it is a limiting one. Bezaleel is named because Aholiab took no part in constructing the furniture of the tabernacle; his share was confined to the coverings, the veil, the curtains and the priests’ dresses, for which Ellicott refers to Exodus 38:23.

Wesley reproduces Henry’s explanation of the repetition almost word for word — the people were not admitted to see these ornaments, the priests only, so they had to be described at length — and then adds two things of his own. First, the narrative shows the care Moses and his workmen took to make everything exactly according to the pattern shewed him in the mount, so that he appeals to every reader concerning his fidelity to him that appointed him, and teaches us to respect all God’s commandments down to every jot and tittle. Second, he reads the ark, the mercy seat and the cherubim as one figure of the glory of a holy God, the sincerity of a holy heart, and the communion between them by a Mediator: God dwells between the cherubim attended by angels whose swiftness the wings signify and whose unanimity appears in their faces being turned one toward another; the upright heart, like the ark, keeps the law of God hid within it; and Christ the great propitiation interposes between us and God’s displeasure.

debates: Why the account is repeated at all. Henry and Wesley explain it by the readers’ need — the laity never saw these things, and what must be taken in is written more than once. Calvin explains it by the wording instead: the near-identity of command and execution is the proof that nothing was altered, and the repetition exists to commend obedience rather than to inform.

Whether Bezaleel worked alone. Gill records the Jewish opinion that he made the ark without help and rejects it, since the same form of words covers objects he can only have overseen. Ellicott reaches a narrower version of the same conclusion from Exodus 38:23: Aholiab was genuinely excluded from the furniture, though not from the fabric work.
outliers: Wesley is the only witness here who reads the ark, mercy seat and cherubim typologically, as a figure of God’s glory, the upright heart and the Mediator between them; the others keep to the questions of authorship and of why the narrative repeats.
themes: why the account repeats the command
obedience as the foundation of piety
nothing added to what was enjoined
Bezaleel named for the whole work

what the priests saw and the people did not

10.pericope_label: And he made the table of shittim wood: two cubits was the length thereof, and a cubit the breadth thereof, and a cubit and a half the height thereof:

schools.summary: Henry carries this verse almost alone, and takes both pieces of furniture together. The table of shewbread shows God to be a good householder who keeps a plentiful table — providence spreading one for all the creatures in the world, grace spreading one for believers in the church — but the shew-bread was to be looked upon rather than fed upon, and eaten afterwards only by the priests, where Christ’s table in the new covenant invites all real Christians to eat. What the law gave a sight of at a distance the gospel gives the enjoyment of. The candlestick he reads from its material: beaten work of pure gold and not wood overlaid, signifying the light of divine revelation that has always enlightened the church, fed with fresh oil from Christ the good Olive; God’s manifestations here are candle-light beside the daylight of the future state. The Bible is that golden candlestick, lighting every part of the tabernacle so the spiritual priests may minister. He notes that it carried knops and flowers for ornament as well as bowls for use, takes them as a figure of adornments in God’s word for which no reason can be given yet which were added for a good purpose, and closes by urging readers to bless God for it and to dread its removal out of its place.

Wesley’s note on this verse reproduces Henry’s treatment of the table rather than supplementing it. He makes the same contrast between the dispensations in nearly the same words — shew-bread to be looked upon and not fed upon, eaten afterwards by the priests only, against a table to which all good Christians are invited guests — quotes the same invitation, Eat, O friends, come eat of my bread, and ends with the same judgment, that what the law gave a sight of at a distance the gospel gives the enjoyment of.

debates: There is no disagreement to record on this verse. The two witnesses who comment on it hold the same position in the same language, and the interest of the pairing is textual rather than exegetical: Wesley’s note is a condensation of Henry’s paragraph, which is why the section has only one line of interpretation running through it.
outliers: Henry alone extends the reading past use to ornament, arguing from the candlestick’s knops and flowers that God has adorned his word with features whose purpose we cannot state but may trust; none of the other witnesses on this chapter draws a doctrinal point from decoration.
themes: God as householder of the world and the church
bread looked upon and bread enjoyed
revelation as light in the tabernacle
fresh oil from Christ the good Olive
ornament as well as use in the sanctuary
